strengths: The paper studies an interesting problem in average-reward RL, leverages a structural property specific to average-reward MDPs, introduces a generic framework, applies it to CVaR RL, and removes the need to solve bi-level optimization problems explicitly.
The paper is mostly well-organized and well-written, with helpful figures that illustrate concepts.
The paper includes numerical experiments, and the two domains used for the experiments sound interesting and relevant to showcase the framework.
The abstract, introduction, and preliminaries on average reward reinforcement learning are well-written and clearly presented.

The TD and Q-learning with stochastic approximation algorithms, along with Theorems 4.1–4.3, appear to be rigorously verified with proofs in Appendix B, effectively extending results from [1, 2, 3] to the multi-subtasks setting.
The paper is easy to read, and the writing skills are good.
The work appears original in proposing CVaR optimization for the average reward criterion, as no prior work is known.
weaknesses: The paper effectively assumes a unichain condition for both prediction and control, which is a significant limitation because many real-world systems do not satisfy this assumption; the analysis relies on a unique stationary distribution that is not guaranteed without the unichain assumption.
The presented framework only shows asymptotic convergence (in the tabular case) and lacks non-asymptotic bounds, making it difficult to assess finite-time performance and convergence rates.

The use of an augmented state-space for CVaR RL is presented as a standard technique, but the paper does not discuss whether the “augmented but highly structured” state-space can be leveraged to improve computational efficiency or sample complexity, nor does it compare to existing methods that exploit such structure.

Equation 19 in Section 5 lacks a clear explanation of the choice of function f; the paper should provide a more detailed justification of the subtask function, its motivation, properties, and impact on algorithm performance.

It is unclear whether RED performs simultaneous learning of multiple subtasks without any sacrifice; the paper should explicitly state any trade‑offs or limitations associated with learning multiple subtasks simultaneously.
The term “subtask” may cause confusion with hierarchical RL terminology and may not accurately reflect its role; alternative naming should be considered.

The literature review is rather weak; the paper should provide broader coverage of related work in risk‑sensitive RL (including discounted and episodic settings) and discuss how the proposed approach compares to existing methods.
The preliminary section on average‑reward MDPs and RL is overly long; compressing Section 3.1 would free space for more novel contributions.
Figures are not readable.

The paper shows limited engagement with prior work on risk‑aware average‑reward MDPs, inaccurately claims novelty, and overlooks several existing approaches that avoid state‑space augmentation and use stationary Markov policies.

The CVaR analysis in Appendix C.1 focuses only on evaluation and does not provide analysis for policy optimization; the average‑criterion CVaR objective is not explicitly presented, and Sections 4 and 5 feel disconnected.

Empirical results do not demonstrate that the algorithm effectively optimizes the desired CVaR risk level; the experiments lack training across multiple risk levels and comparisons with other approaches under an average‑reward criterion.

The claim of learning a CVaR‑optimizing policy without a bi‑level optimization scheme or augmented state-space is not substantiated; computational complexity or running‑time comparisons with prior methods are missing.

The significance of the work is questionable because analytical advantages of the average‑reward criterion in the risk‑neutral case suggest that similar challenges may exist for risk‑sensitive MDPs, weakening the contribution.
Missing related work: [5] on infinite‑horizon average reward with entropic risk is not cited.
The paper lacks a discussion of whether the risk considered is nested or static, and does not address potential time‑consistency issues.
Initial claims in Section 2.1 are inaccurate; average criteria have been extensively studied since the 1960s (e.g., Howard and Blackwell), and equations (4)-(5) are actually Poisson equations.
The paper does not consider function approximation for CVaR, although related work does so for the risk‑neutral case.
Definition 4.1 is unclear and its relation to the max in Eq. (10) is not explained.
Statements of Theorems 4.1 and 4.2 are vague, lacking formalization and justification for focusing on multiple subtasks rather than a single CVaR subtask.
The paper should include formal algorithm pseudo‑codes instead of a list of equations (17).
Learning rates η and α are inconsistently defined (sometimes constant, sometimes time‑ or state‑dependent) without clear rationale.
Convergence plots appear to show only a single run per experiment; the authors should provide mean ± std error curves over multiple seeds.
The writing is vague, making it hard to understand why subtasks are introduced for the CVaR problem and how equation (19) was derived.
Derivations from 13a to 13b and from 14a to 14b are invalid for piece‑wise linear functions f, raising concerns about the correctness of the theoretical results.

Numerous typographical and factual errors (e.g., misstatement about Puterman, incorrect notation, misuse of “μ_π”, missing superscript vs. sup, inconsistent variable notation) further undermine the paper’s clarity and correctness.
